title: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Opening with Aquinas on reward and punishment, this essay argues that England's school accountability system actively penalizes schools for doing right by 'high cost, high risk' (HCHR) pupils — those with special educational needs or disabilities. Borrowing a framework from medicine, banking, and law, the author argues that any system relying on workforce altruism will fail unless incentives are calibrated to reward the desired behaviour, and that schools are currently rewarded for avoiding, not admitting and retaining, SEND pupils. The piece's central evidence is that Ofsted's new inspection of inclusion appears to grade schools with lower proportions of SEND pupils more favourably, creating an unintended incentive toward admissions barriers or off-rolling, compounded by 'nominal funding' rules that force schools with many high-needs pupils to divert money from general budgets. A second major argument targets the Progress 8 measure, showing it functions less as a measure of school effectiveness than of pupil intake, since lower-prior-attaining pupils typically progress less regardless of school quality — making Progress 8 a poor, noisy proxy that punishes schools serving disadvantaged cohorts. The essay also challenges the widespread assumption that between-school variation drives outcome inequality, noting that inequality within schools is often larger, and calls for early, joined-up, multi-disciplinary intervention rather than accountability systems that wait for struggle to become severe.
points: Argues Ofsted's inclusion inspection appears to reward schools with the lowest proportion of SEND pupils, creating an incentive to reduce admissions of children with additional needs.
Shows 'nominal funding' rules force schools with many high-needs pupils to divert money from general budgets, eroding education quality for the whole school population.
Demonstrates Progress 8 is 'a very noisy measure of comparative school effectiveness' because lower-prior-attaining pupils make less progress regardless of school quality.
Challenges the assumption that between-school variance drives outcome inequality, noting inequality within schools is often greater than between them.
Calls for early, joined-up, multi-disciplinary policy action on cost and risk rather than accountability systems that wait for struggle to become severe.
quotes: An industry which relies upon the moral fortitude of its workforce to act in the best interests of those it serves will inevitably fail unless the system is calibrated to reward desirable behaviours and sanction transgression.

There is evidence emerging that those schools receiving the higher grades for inclusion through inspection are those with the lowest proportion of SEND pupils, and vice versa (as this TES article sets out).

Those schools with disproportionate numbers of high needs pupils must pay for this by diverting funds from general school funding. Local authorities have historically compensated by providing additional funding for schools in this position, but over time these schemes have been eroded meaning schools are left to pick up the bill.

The Progress 8 measure models the ‘distance travelled’ for each pupil from their KS2 starting point. However, what it does not do is to recognise that lower prior attaining pupils tend to make less progress at secondary school than their higher attaining peers.
It is a measure of school impact, but it is a very noisy measure of comparative school effectiveness.

Yet, there is greater inequality within each school than between schools. Two schools with identical Progress 8 scores may have two very different progress profiles: one where progress is consistent across pupils and one where achievement is widely spread.
People within education want to do the right thing but we must stop punishing them for doing so.
